works.title: VibeServe: Can AI Agents Build Bespoke LLM Serving Systems?

publication.actor: Codex CLI; underlying model unspecified
publication.target: Up to Qwen3-32B; H100, L4 and Apple hardware
publication.summary: Generates a serving implementation for a specified model, hardware platform and workload.
details: Concrete task and artifact

VibeServe, whose repository is now named VibeSys, studies six deployment scenarios. Its largest text-model case uses Qwen3-32B on one H100 for predicted-output code editing with CodeEditorBench. Another uses Olmo-Hybrid-7B on one L4 with a shared 32k-token prefix, 128-token suffix, 128-token output and concurrency 20. The deliverable is an executable specialized serving path, with permitted reuse of libraries such as FlashInfer or MLX.
Method and supplied infrastructure

An outer orchestrator maintains an issue backlog, Git checkpoints and Markdown memory. Fresh-context Implementer, Accuracy Judge and Performance Evaluator roles implement, check and profile each change. Skills supply knowledge and implementation references from existing serving systems. Humans provide the deployment requirements, reference implementation and read-only correctness checker. This is an executable workflow around a coding agent; the paper does not train a new model.
Results and comparison

Standard Llama-8B/H100 serving approximately matches vLLM. The Qwen-32B editing case reports 5.95× over vanilla vLLM and about 2× over draft-model speculation. The Olmo case reports 3.45× throughput by sharing both attention KV and DeltaNet state. Other cases report 1.69× ASR TTFT improvement, Mac JSON decoding from 22.1 to 8.6 seconds, and Show-o2 latency from 873 to 687 ms on H100. These use different references and deployment contracts and must not be averaged into one speedup.
Research budget

Appendix A reports role calls and active time: approximately 3–25 hours per scenario. These are neither a complete token ledger nor GPU-hours. The paper acknowledges nontrivial per-target search costs.
Evaluation context

Evaluates single-seed searches across six deployment scenarios. Predicted-output editing, shared recurrent state and permitted image-generation approximations are task-specific conditions. JSON-schema failures are reported. The reviewed paper and current repository use different versions; matched-token harness and skills ablations are outside the reported study.

works.title: SkyDiscover-Synthesize (SkySynth): Building Specialized Systems We Can Trust with Agents

publication.actor: Opus 4.8 in the September report
publication.summary: Synthesizes a specialized engine while strengthening specifications and tests.
details: Concrete task and artifact

The inference case targets repeated sampling with shared long prefixes. The pinned public task specifies BF16 weights and KV cache, non-thinking mode, two 24,576-token roots with 32 branches each, 64 concurrent requests, and 128/256 output tokens through an OpenAI-compatible completions endpoint. PyTorch may be used for validation but not as the production engine; CUDA, Triton and established low-level libraries are allowed.
Method and supplied infrastructure

Spec Builder prepares requirements and environment/workload specifications. Planner, Coding Agent, Evaluator and Critic iterate on implementations; an Auditor looks for violations that improve the score and turns confirmed violations into tests. The public implementation includes a lead SKILL.md, role prompts, Python specification/checkpoint tools, test-validation scripts, delivery hooks and a cross-run knowledge base. In the inspected snapshot, a new adversarial test must pass a trusted reference and reject a corresponding faulty implementation.
Results and comparison

The September report describes approximately 2.2× throughput over tuned vLLM/SGLang for its inference workload. Batched decode amortizes weight reads; grouped cascade attention reuses shared-prefix KV reads. An agent modifying vLLM for roughly seven hours improved 287 to 490 tokens/s, still below the synthesized engine. A candidate that silently truncated context to 1,000 tokens illustrates why checking short inputs alone is insufficient.
Research budget
No complete inference-specific token/GPU-hour comparison was established. The report’s KV-store development costs must not be assigned to the inference case.
Evaluation context

The inference entry refers to the September blog/code case on one Qwen3-4B model and one L4. The May JIT/Jitskit paper and the 95.2% formal-verification result concern storage systems. Fixed test prompts use exact outputs; other prompts permit near-tie variation. Repository contracts can change across versions.

works.title: SGLang Agent-Assisted Development: Skills and Real Serving Patches

publication.scope: Changes to an existing serving stack
publication.actor: Claude Code / Codex; exact underlying models not consistently reported
publication.summary: Public skills and merged patches document concrete agent-assisted serving development.
details: Concrete task and artifact

PR #28744 modifies both router and engine for DeepSeek-V4-Flash with seven engines and 60k/ 125k-token prefixes; the hardware is not disclosed in the inspected evidence. PR #22664 has a clearer hardware contract: Qwen3-Coder-Next, four H100s, TP=4, 2,048 input tokens, 256 output tokens, 128 requests and concurrency 32. Both deliver patches to an existing system.
Method and supplied infrastructure

Skills cover CUDA debugging, serving benchmarks, profiler analysis, pipeline analysis and a Humanize loop. They encode preflight checks, executable measurement procedures, artifact formats and review gates. A typical loop produces a plan, has Claude Code implement/benchmark/commit changes, and has Codex review the evidence before continuing. Maintainers set goals and review final changes; a single-agent Goal variant is also described.
Results and comparison

PR #28744 tokenizes once at the Rust ingress, uses token IDs for cache-aware routing and forwards them to engines to avoid duplicate work, with fallbacks for unsupported inputs. Reported TTFT reductions are 29%/ 41% at idle and 34–49% under selected loads. PR #22664 increases throughput from 5.49 to 9.41 requests/s (+71.4%); TTFT falls from 456.24 to 167.54 ms and TPOT from 50.41 to 25.49 ms. Its patch enables an existing FlashInfer all-reduce fusion path for the architecture; it does not invent a new collective.
Research budget
No complete experiment-wide token ledger or matched-budget skills ablation. Lower orchestration overhead in a workflow description is not itself measured token savings.
Evaluation context

The reported artifacts are merged patches to an existing serving stack. The fusion evaluation includes MMLU/GSM8K comparisons. Hardware and model examples in the blog are distinguished from the measured PR configurations.

works.title: Asari: automated inference optimization

publication.scope: Changes to an existing serving stack
publication.actor: Optimization actor not disclosed
publication.summary: Optimizes mature large-model serving across kernels, scheduling and configuration.
details: Concrete task and artifact
The target is end-to-end inference for two large models at multiple concurrency levels on eight B200s. The artifact is a modified vLLM stack, not a newly synthesized server.
Method and supplied infrastructure

A discover/build → evaluate → verify → self-improve loop combines profiling, static inspection and accumulated experience. Hierarchical microbenchmarks and end-to-end tests shorten feedback cycles. Token-distribution checks on multilingual C4 prompts compare optimized and stock execution. The workflow is described publicly, but the proprietary agent and its skills are not sufficiently exposed for full reconstruction.
Results and comparison

The report gives up to 16% improvement in throughput and interactivity against matched vLLM baselines. Client/server configuration affects absolute values, so results should be compared within each setup. One transfer example reuses a deadlock lesson from DeepSeek to GLM and avoids about 44 minutes of waiting.
Research budget
Approximately one day of optimization per concurrency setting; total tokens, failed attempts and all-in GPU-hours are not fully disclosed.
Evaluation context

Evaluates a combined optimization workflow against a mature serving baseline with distribution checks. A deadlock-lesson transfer is one reported example; separate contributions from accumulated experience, search and human input are not isolated in this study.

works.title: GLM builds its inference infrastructure

publication.actor: GLM-5.3 researcher (~753B total parameters)
publication.summary: Reports substantial gains during human–AI development of production infrastructure.
details: Concrete task and artifact

The report describes production inference engineering involving CPU/GPU coordination, KV transfer and attention implementation. Its deployment discussion refers to roughly 100k devices; this is deployment scale, not the size of the agent’s experimental allocation.
Method and supplied infrastructure

Human engineers and GLM diagnose bottlenecks, modify implementations and validate changes. Public material does not provide a complete reproducible skills library, orchestration implementation or set of research prompts. One case traces KV-transfer gaps to CPU-side behavior including Python/GIL effects.
Results and comparison

The vendor reports approximately 3× throughput from the initial implementation to production in under two weeks. A local KV-transfer idle-gap fraction falls from over 20% to under 1%. The two measurements have different denominators.
Research budget
Project duration is reported, but the agent’s total tokens, GPU-hours, failed experiments and human intervention are not fully itemized.
Evaluation context

The source is a production engineering report combining AI assistance, expert work and serving-stack development. The catalog review uses the official indexed text; the locally archived HTML does not contain the full article.

works.title: FlashVector

publication.scope: Changes across an existing recommendation stack
publication.actor: Actor model not adequately disclosed
publication.target: Unity recommendation serving; RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell
publication.summary: Optimizes kernels, model graphs, the model server and CPU feature processing.
details: Concrete task and artifact

The examined ranking workload uses FP16/AOTInductor, an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell and batches of 2,000 per request. Other cases modify NVIDIA Triton’s C++ server and a Python feature-processing backend. The target is recommendation serving, not autoregressive text-model inference.
Method and supplied infrastructure

Expert-authored cookbooks and profiling guidance inform a loop that selects a layer, profiles it, diagnoses a bottleneck, implements a change and verifies the full local path. Accepted changes are retained; a refinement step records experience. The harness also handles measurement noise and applying/undoing patches. It does not optimize all four layers simultaneously in every iteration.
Results and comparison

A two-tower retrieval case moves string-input conversion from Python to C++, reporting a 30× local improvement. A ranking case exposes embedding operations to AOTInductor fusion and reuses duplicate embeddings. One reported ranking configuration reaches about 2× throughput and 1.98× latency improvement; CPU feature processing reports about 1.6×. These cannot be multiplied into a system-wide figure.
Research budget
No complete LLM-token budget was established. The paper discusses stabilizing measurements, including reducing observed noise through additional samples.
Evaluation context

The workloads concern recommendation serving and span multiple software layers. Local serialization measurements and full-path serving measurements have different scopes. Agent search and expert cookbooks are used together in the reported workflow.

works.title: RoofLang: Enabling AI-Driven Architecting of LLM Inference Systems

publication.actor: DeepSeek-V4-Pro; V4-Flash for lightweight/subagent work
publication.target: Simulated B300 configurations, up to 256 GPUs in the agent cases
publication.summary: Searches legal computation, placement and communication graphs before implementation.
details: Concrete task and artifact

The largest illustrated agent case models DeepSeek-V4-Pro decode at 64k context on 256 B300s, batch 4,096, EP=16 and PP=16. Another models 1M-token prefill on 16 B300s. The output is a transformed graph, placement and simulated trace—not a running B300 serving implementation.
Method and supplied infrastructure

RoofLang supplies compute/hardware graphs, constrained placement and semantics-preserving graph transformations, and a roofline-based discrete-event simulator. A persistent Claude Code process uses DeepSeek models, reads the repository and baseline results, proposes changes, checks legality and consumes simulation feedback. The specialized DSL and evaluator are central; a large skill library is not the main contribution.
Results and comparison

Changing the 256-GPU pipeline partition from (4×13, 3×3) to (3, 4×14, 2) accounts for embedding/output-head costs and improves simulated throughput/interactivity by 20.3%. Expert splitting gives 6.23% in an eight-B300 prefill case; node-local expert replication gives 50.1% in the 16-B300 long-context case. Cross-model peak-throughput comparisons are separate from these agent-search gains.
Research budget

The persistent loop has no preset turn limit and stops at the agent’s discretion. No complete comparable token/search budget is reported. Large simulations can themselves require hours and substantial host memory.
Evaluation context

Results use analytical simulation with assumptions about MoE balance and execution overlap. Initial workload and hardware graphs are supplied externally. Real-hardware measurements and calibration of omitted execution costs are separate evaluation steps.

works.title: Glia: A Human-Inspired AI for Automated Systems Design and Optimization

publication.actor: o3; GPT-5 for adaptation
publication.summary: Generates system policies, with both simulator results and a manually integrated real-stack transfer.
details: Concrete task and artifact

The largest adaptation task uses Vidur to simulate Llama3.3-70B FP8 on eight H100s, 200 concurrent requests and a P90 TTFT constraint below 1,500 ms while maximizing QPS. The real-stack experiment uses Llama3-8B on four A10s in vLLM ProductionStack.
Method and supplied infrastructure

A Researcher reads code, proposes hypotheses and runs experiments. A Supervisor observes the research process and results, asks questions and redirects work without direct code access. Humans supply the environment, simulator and objective. MultiContext variants restart search contexts; they are not equivalent to Engram’s persistent research archive.
Results and comparison

The main routing simulation reports 2.2× lower response time than least-loaded queue and 1.6× versus OpenEvolve. At 7.5 QPS, the real-stack transfer reports over 4.5× lower slowdown than LLQ; slowdown is response time relative to an idealized reference, not throughput. The 70B adaptation meets its SLO in 10/10 simulated trials.
Research budget
Some configurations use about $30 per run and 15 or 100 simulator evaluations. Evaluation counts and dollar limits are not a complete token-normalized comparison.
Evaluation context

The smaller-model routing policy is evaluated on real hardware with human integration; the larger-model adaptation is simulated. Agent and human development-time comparisons use different budget conditions.

works.title: Improving Coherence and Persistence in Agentic AI for System Optimization

publication.scope: Persistent research memory for policy search
publication.actor: o3; GPT-5.2 in some sensitivity experiments
publication.summary: Uses an Archive and Research Digest to sustain research across fresh agent contexts.
details: Concrete task and artifact

The inference-related tasks include request routing under Vidur and input reordering for LLM-SQL across five datasets. The artifact is a policy program and research history, not a new engine or updated model weights.
Method and supplied infrastructure

Fresh-context researchers read a compact Digest, retrieve detailed code/experiments from an Archive, formulate hypotheses, edit programs, run an evaluator and write a handoff. The Digest records insights, failures and next steps. This is persistent research state around task-specific evaluators, rather than a serving-specific skills library.
Results and comparison

For routing, ten seeds with 100 evaluations per run yield mean best response time of 23.9 seconds versus 25.7 for Glia and 39.2 for OpenEvolve. LLM-SQL scores are 0.721 versus 0.719 and 0.714. The latter score combines 95% cache-hit contribution with a 5% runtime bonus; it is not a throughput ratio.
Research budget
Matching 100 evaluations does not match the tokens used to read, summarize and retrieve research history. A complete inference-specific token ledger was not established in this review.
Evaluation context

Routing is evaluated in simulation. Reported policy scores, their uncertainty and supplied preprocessing define the inference-related comparison; broader network-optimization tasks have separate objectives.

works.title: Let the Barbarians In: How AI Can Accelerate Systems Research

publication.actor: GPT-5 / Gemini 3 Pro Preview
publication.target: EPLB, model placement and LLM-SQL among ten systems tasks
publication.summary: Packages systems research into editable programs with executable evaluators.
details: Concrete task and artifact

Inference-related tasks include MoE expert load balancing, Prism model-to-GPU placement and LLM-SQL input ordering. The output is a heuristic or algorithm inside a fixed interface, not a complete inference runtime.
Method and supplied infrastructure

Humans provide a seed program, API, problem description and evaluator returning quality, runtime or cost feedback. Existing systems such as OpenEvolve, GEPA and ShinkaEvolve generate and select candidates. The contribution is the research formulation and task harness rather than a new frontier researcher or inference-specific skill library.
Results and comparison

EPLB reports comparable balance with an approximately 13× faster placement algorithm. Prism reports about 20.9% lower benchmark cost than a published human solution. LLM-SQL reports roughly 3–3.9× faster reordering with similar cache hit rates. None is a direct claim that served LLM tokens became faster by the same factor.
Research budget

Typical experiments use 100 iterations and three repeats. Example task budgets report around five hours/≤$15 for EPLB and one hour/≤$15–20 for Prism/LLM-SQL. These do not replace a full token accounting.
Evaluation context

The ten-task suite includes inference-related and other systems tasks. Modeled placement cost, optimizer runtime and deployed token latency measure different quantities. Task interfaces, objectives and domain hints are supplied by the benchmark.

works.title: AdaEvolve: Adaptive LLM-Driven Zeroth-Order Optimization (SkyDiscover)

publication.actor: GPT-5 / Gemini 3 Pro
publication.summary: Adapts exploration and search-budget allocation across populations of candidate programs.
details: Concrete task and artifact

AdaEvolve evaluates EPLB, Prism and LLM-SQL among broader systems tasks. The resulting artifacts are optimized policy functions and search histories. SkyDiscover is the framework; SkySynth is a separate subsequent system-synthesis branch.
Method and supplied infrastructure

ContextBuilder, SolutionGenerator, Evaluator and Selector organize code evolution. Within islands, improvement history adjusts exploration; UCB allocates effort across islands, and stagnation can trigger new high-level guidance. A task supplies evaluator.py, a seed/configuration and a problem description.
Results and comparison

With GPT-5, LLM-SQL scores 0.746±0.03 versus OpenEvolve’s 0.710±0.01; Prism scores 26.30 versus 26.23, and EPLB 0.134 versus 0.127. These are task-specific scores, not comparable throughput or dollar figures.
Research budget
ADRS experiments use 100 iterations and three repeats. A fixed iteration count does not equalize prompt lengths, candidate generation costs or evaluator runtime.
Evaluation context
The reviewed results concern policy search in AdaEvolve v1. Later SkyDiscover-family methods and framework versions have separate results and configurations.

works.title: InferenceBench

publication.actor: 15 frontier agent configurations; best aggregate: Sonnet 4.6
publication.summary: Tests whether an agent can deliver a working, faster inference endpoint within two hours.
details: Concrete task and artifact

Each run starts from an empty directory with a target model, one H100 and an OpenAI-compatible endpoint contract. Four scenarios emphasize TTFT, TPOT, concurrent throughput or a combined objective. The main study comprises 15 configurations × four scenarios × three seeds.
Method and supplied infrastructure

The environment supplies hardware, model access and quality/performance evaluators. Agents select frameworks, attention backends, quantization and runtime settings. The final deliverable must launch and serve requests; 169 of 180 runs ultimately use vLLM. Starting from an empty directory therefore usually means assembling/configuring an existing stack rather than synthesizing a new runtime.
Results and comparison

The best agent reaches an aggregate 8.08× over eager, compared with 4.05× for default vLLM. Under the same wall-clock budget, SMAC reaches 11.53×, TPE 11.25× and random search 10.20×. Best-seen and final submissions differ when a last change breaks delivery.
Research budget
Two hours and one H100 per run. This controls elapsed time and available hardware, not total tokens or an identical configuration-search space.
Evaluation context

Uses single-GPU 7B serving and a quality gate retaining at least 95% of baseline MMLU-Pro performance on 500 questions. The source reports May 20 while the arXiv identifier begins 2607; the first-release month remains unresolved.

works.title: ISO-Bench

publication.actor: Claude Code / Sonnet 4.5; Codex / GPT-5; TRAE; Gemini judge
publication.summary: Reconstructs real serving performance work from merged patches.
details: Concrete task and artifact

Tasks reset repositories to the state before a real optimization PR and ask an agent to address the issue. The deliverable is a patch to a functioning serving stack; this tests repository engineering rather than greenfield engine synthesis.
Method and supplied infrastructure

The benchmark supplies repository state, problem descriptions and execution tests. Coding harnesses implement changes; semantic assessment complements measured performance. Task construction and executable evaluation are the main contribution, not a new inference-research agent.
Results and comparison

Execution success varies by setup, including 46.2% for Claude Code on vLLM and 86.7% for TRAE/GPT-5 on SGLang; these are not speedup percentages. A concrete successful case moves reshape outside a FlashAttention custom op and gains 21.09% throughput. Another Bamba-9B case gets faster while accuracy collapses from 32 to 0, illustrating why performance alone is insufficient.
Research budget
A complete normalized token/GPU-hour comparison was not established in the reviewed material.
Evaluation context

Tasks originate in public PRs, so possible prior exposure is relevant to evaluation design. Reference-patch grading, alternative valid solutions, execution success, correctness and acceleration are separate comparison dimensions.

works.title: AMD Apex

publication.actor: Configurable coding-agent backend
publication.summary: Connects serving profiles to kernel generation, validation and reintegration.
details: Concrete task and artifact

The repository documents a registry of 17 inference configurations, including GPT-OSS-120B. This establishes available task entry points, not a verified successful 120B optimization experiment. The artifact is a reusable optimization environment.
Method and supplied infrastructure

Benchmark the full service, rank hot kernels, ask an LLM to edit HIP/Python, then compile and check correctness/performance through Magpie. A local gain above 1.05× permits hotpatching into the dependency installation, followed by an end-to-end retest. Domain skills, ROCm documentation/MCP tools, ground-truth specifications and cache isolation support the loop.
Results and comparison

The principal verified contribution here is the public workflow and implementation. No unified controlled result table was established that would justify a general serving speedup or research-efficiency claim.
Research budget
Backends and run configurations vary; no fixed-model, fixed-budget comparative experiment was established.
Evaluation context

The entry describes a configurable implementation and its available interfaces. Actor choice and optimization outcomes depend on run configuration. February denotes repository creation; no confirmed paper release date is assigned.
